resources.string: Gramvousa chamomile
Anthemis glaberrima
Gramvousa chamomile

A rare, nearly hairless annual endemic to the Gramvousa islets. Finely divided leaves and small daisy heads with white rays around a yellow disc distinguish it from common chamomiles. Critically endangered and restricted to a tiny coastal range.
Endemic to the Gramvousa islets, Crete, Greece.
Low, branched annual, commonly just a few centimetres tall.
Alternate, glabrous leaves, entire to deeply divided.
Small daisy heads with white rays and a yellow disc.
Dry grooved achene; not fleshy.
Syrian rue
Peganum harmala
Syrian rue; harmal

Drought-adapted perennial with divided leaves, solitary white flowers and rounded three-chambered capsules. All parts contain biologically active alkaloids and can be toxic; this description is for recognition, not food or medicinal use.
Mediterranean region east through western and central Asia to Mongolia and the Indian subcontinent; widely introduced.
Much-branched perennial, erect to spreading, generally under one metre.
Alternate grey-green leaves divided into narrow linear segments.
Solitary white five-petalled flowers with yellow anthers.
Rounded three-chambered capsule with many angular seeds.
Sea plantain
Plantago maritima
Sea plantain

Salt-tolerant perennial in a compact basal rosette. Its narrow, fleshy, often channelled leaves differ from broad-leaved plantains; leafless scapes carry short cylindrical spikes of tiny greenish flowers.
European and North African coasts and northern Asia, with scattered northern American populations.
Compact basal rosette with leafless flowering scapes.
Narrow, fleshy, often channelled linear leaves.
Tiny greenish flowers tightly packed in a short cylindrical spike.
Small dry capsule containing a few seeds.
Hoary plantain
Plantago media
Hoary plantain; broad-leaved plantain

Rosette perennial distinguished from Plantago major by shorter, often softly hairy leaves and pinkish flowers whose long white stamens project conspicuously. Several strong ribs run down each blade into its petiole.
Europe across temperate Asia to Iran; common in open and often calcareous grassland.
Basal rosette with a short upright flowering stalk.
Broadly elliptic, ribbed, often softly hairy leaves.
Pinkish flowers in a dense spike; white stamens protrude.
Dry capsules release several small seeds.
Pink knotweed
Persicaria capitata
Pink knotweed; pink-headed persicaria

Creeping mat-forming perennial with oval leaves often marked by a dark V and spherical pink flower heads. Many small flowers form each head, unlike the slender spikes of numerous related knotweeds; it can spread readily in warm climates.
Himalaya and adjacent Indian subcontinent and southwestern China; cultivated and naturalised elsewhere.
Prostrate stems root at nodes and form a dense mat.
Alternate oval leaves, often with a dark V-shaped mark.
Many tiny pink flowers form rounded terminal heads.
Small dry achene enclosed by persistent floral parts.
Korean cherry
Prunus maximowiczii
Korean cherry; Maximowicz cherry

Small deciduous East Asian tree with elliptic sharply toothed leaves. Short corymbs of white spring flowers are followed by small drupes that ripen from red to nearly black, helping separate it from pink-flowered ornamental cherries.
Russian Far East, northeastern China, Korea and Japan; woodland margins and thickets.
Small deciduous tree with spreading branches and rounded crown.
Alternate elliptic leaves with sharply toothed margins.
White five-petalled flowers in short corymbs.
Ovoid drupe, red then deep purple-black when ripe.
Chacruna
Psychotria viridis
Chacruna

Evergreen tropical understory shrub with opposite glossy leaves, interpetiolar stipules and small terminal clusters of pale flowers. Small fleshy fruits follow flowering. Identification should use the full combination of foliage and inflorescence, not a common name alone.
Humid tropical South America, especially the Amazonian region; also cultivated.
Evergreen shrub or small tree of shaded humid forest.
Opposite glossy entire leaves with stipules between petioles.
Small pale flowers in branched terminal clusters.
Small fleshy berries, green then often red or dark.
Common saltmarsh grass
Puccinellia maritima
Common saltmarsh grass

Perennial grass of saline marshes, spreading by creeping stolons or rhizomes into low turf. Narrow leaves and open delicate panicles are characteristic; each spikelet bears several tiny florets and a dry grain.
Atlantic and northern European coasts, especially western and northern saltmarshes.
Low turf with creeping stolons and flowering culms.
Narrow flat to folded blades, often blue-green.
Open panicle of small multi-flowered spikelets.
Dry caryopsis enclosed by persistent floral bracts.
Yellow rattle
Rhinanthus minor
Yellow rattle

Annual hemiparasite of grassland. Opposite toothed leaves accompany yellow two-lipped flowers within an inflated toothed calyx; mature dry capsules rattle. Similar Rhinanthus species can be difficult to separate without close floral inspection.
Much of Europe and western Asia to Siberia; meadows and open grassland.
Slender annual with opposite branches and flowering spike.
Opposite sessile leaves with sharp teeth.
Yellow bilabiate corolla in an inflated toothed calyx.
Inflated dry capsule containing rattling seeds.
Staghorn sumac
Rhus typhina
Staghorn sumac; velvet sumac

Deciduous North American shrub or small tree with young branches densely velvety. Large pinnate leaves have many serrated leaflets; small flowers form upright clusters and mature into red hairy fruit cones. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants.
Eastern Canada and eastern United States; widely planted elsewhere.
Multi-stemmed shrub or small tree with velvety young shoots.
Large pinnate leaves with many sharply toothed leaflets.
Small yellow-green flowers in dense upright panicles.
Persistent upright clusters of red hairy drupes.
Musk rose
Rosa moschata
Musk rose

Scrambling or climbing rose with long arching canes and clusters of strongly musk-scented, usually single white flowers. Pinnate toothed leaves precede small orange-red hips. Taxonomic limits and wild origin of musk roses vary between authorities.
Kew gives southern Iran to Afghanistan as native range; long cultivated elsewhere.
Long arching canes form a scrambling shrub or climber.
Pinnate leaves commonly bear five to seven toothed leaflets.
White single flowers in clusters, with yellow stamens and musk scent.
Small orange-red hips containing many achenes.
Toothbrush tree
Salvadora persica
Toothbrush tree; miswak tree

Drought-tolerant, much-branched shrub or small tree with opposite somewhat fleshy leaves, tiny greenish-yellow flowers and red-purple drupes. Twigs have a documented traditional use as chewing sticks; this does not establish that all parts are safe to eat.
Arid Africa and Arabian Peninsula east to South Asia; dry scrub and saline ground.
Evergreen, spreading shrub or small tree with many branches.
Opposite, entire elliptic leaves, leathery to somewhat succulent.
Tiny greenish-yellow flowers in branched clusters.
Small fleshy drupes ripen red to purple.
Tansy
Tanacetum vulgare
Tansy; common tansy

Aromatic rhizomatous perennial with finely divided leaves and flat-topped clusters of yellow button heads. Unlike a typical daisy, the heads lack white rays. The plant contains toxic compounds, particularly in concentrated preparations, and is not presented as food.
Europe and temperate Asia; introduced and naturalised across other temperate regions.
Erect aromatic perennial arising from spreading rhizomes.
Alternate leaves deeply divided into narrow toothed segments.
Yellow button heads in flat clusters; no white ray florets.
Dry achene with no conspicuous pappus.
Small nettle
Urtica urens
Small nettle; burning nettle

Small annual nettle, usually with one main stem and opposite toothed leaves. Stinging hairs occur on leaves and stems. Unlike perennial Urtica dioica, both sexes often occur in the same axillary clusters. Do not touch: hairs inject irritants.
Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia; widely introduced in disturbed soils.
Small erect annual, simple or sparsely branched.
Opposite ovate leaves with coarse teeth and stinging hairs.
Tiny green flowers in short axillary clusters, often both sexes together.
Tiny dry one-seeded achene enclosed by persistent perianth.
Oval-leaf blueberry
Vaccinium ovalifolium
Oval-leaf blueberry; oval-leaf bilberry

Shrub of cool moist forests, deciduous to semi-evergreen. Alternate oval leaves are finely toothed; pink urn-shaped flowers mature into blue-black berries with a waxy bloom. It is a northern relative of familiar blueberries.
Northern Pacific region from northeastern Asia to Alaska and western North America.
Low to medium branched woodland shrub.
Alternate oval leaves with fine teeth, often red before falling.
Pink urn-shaped flowers singly or in small clusters.
Blue-black berry covered by a pale waxy bloom.
Rose apple
Syzygium jambos
Rose apple

Evergreen tropical tree with opposite glossy narrow leaves, pale flowers bearing many long stamens, and fragrant pale fruits shaped like bells or pears. Cultivated for fruit and shade; introduced populations are invasive on some islands.
Native to Southeast Asia; widely cultivated and naturalised throughout the tropics.
Evergreen small to medium tree with a dense crown.
Opposite lanceolate glossy leaves with translucent oil glands.
Pale flowers with a conspicuous tuft of long white stamens.
Fragrant pale yellow to pink bell- or pear-shaped fruit.
Siamese rough bush
Streblus asper
Siamese rough bush

Small evergreen Asian tree with milky latex and very rough stiff leaves. Tiny male flowers form compact globose heads; separate female flowers develop into yellow-orange drupes. The sandpapery leaf surface is a useful identification character.
South and Southeast Asia, from India and Sri Lanka through Indochina to Malesia.
Irregularly branched evergreen small tree with milky latex.
Alternate elliptic leaves with rough sandpapery surface and toothed edge.
Tiny unisexual flowers; male clusters are globose and axillary.
Small yellow to orange fleshy drupe.
Loneliest palm
Hyophorbe amaricaulis
Loneliest palm; palmier solitaire de Curepipe

Critically endangered Mauritian palm represented by one known cultivated survivor at Curepipe Botanic Gardens. It has a slender solitary trunk and pinnate crown. Sources disagree about trunk swelling; this plate follows recent accounts distinguishing it from the bottle palm H. lagenicaulis.
Endemic to Mauritius; no confirmed wild population remains, one cultivated survivor documented at Curepipe.
Solitary tall slender palm with a small crown of arching fronds.
Pinnate fronds with many narrow leaflets along a central rachis.
Small flowers on an inflorescence beneath the crown; rarely observed.
Small ovoid palm fruits; poorly documented for the survivor.
Hairy-fruited mistletoe cactus
Rhipsalis pilocarpa
Hairy-fruited mistletoe cactus

Epiphytic cactus with slender cylindrical branching stems, fine bristles on areoles, fragrant white flowers near shoot tips and red bristly fruits. True broad leaves are absent; photosynthesis occurs in the green stems.
Humid Atlantic forests of southeastern Brazil; epiphytic on branches.
Pendant epiphytic cactus with slender branching cylindrical stems.
True leaves absent; green stems bear small bristly areoles.
Small fragrant white flowers near stem tips.
Rounded red berry densely covered with fine bristles.
Haraella
Haraella retrocalla
Haraella retrocalla; Gastrochilus retrocallus

Miniature monopodial epiphytic orchid from Taiwan, with a short stem, two-ranked fleshy leaves and a yellow flower marked red with a fiddle-shaped lip. Kew treats this name as a synonym of Gastrochilus retrocallus, while regional floras retain Haraella; the tree name is retained here.
Taiwan; epiphytic in humid montane forest.
Miniature monopodial epiphyte with a very short stem.
Few fleshy leaves arranged in two ranks.
Small yellow flower with red markings and fiddle-shaped lip.
Slender orchid capsule with dust-like seeds.
Nitrariaceae
A small family including Peganum, often adapted to dry environments.
Nitraria family
Salvadoraceae
Tropical shrubs and trees, commonly with opposite leaves and small flowers.
Salvadora family
Orobanchaceae
A diverse family including root-parasitic and hemiparasitic herbs such as Rhinanthus.
Broomrape family
